reason: These are plausible authorities on the soul (Steuco, Soto, Cano, Aquinas, Coler). Leaving Tholosanus, Peresius and Dandinus unexpanded is a careful choice, and 'probable' is a fair hedge on the Pico reading.
In Apologeticum 22 Tertullian says demons cause diseases and then appear to cure them.
Thyraeus wrote De daemoniacis, De locis infestis and De terrificationibus nocturnis, and Menghi wrote Flagellum daemonum, so the expansion is correct.
Lavater's De spectris is arranged in parts and chapters. Part 1 is about ghosts that are seen and heard, which fits.
Sigismund Scherertz wrote a book on spectres (Libellus consolatorius de spectris), and part 1, chapter 9 is a plausible place for this story.
Joubert's Paradoxa are arranged in decades, and the citation fits a physician arguing from Galen.
Cardano's De rerum varietate has 17 books, so the reference is to the right work.
Sallustio Salviani wrote Variarum lectionum de re medica libri. The title is given in a shortened form but correctly identified.
Gregor Nymann's oration on imagination (Wittenberg, 1613) and Johannes Voschius's De peste are both correctly identified.
Psalm 55:4 matches: 'my heart is sore pained within me: and the terrors of death are fallen upon me.'
In Gordon's Lilium medicinae, particula 2 covers diseases of the head, and chapter 19 deals with mania and melancholy.
Pontano's De rebus coelestibus is in 14 books, so book 10 is a valid place.
Burton himself names Perkins's Cases of Conscience in the same sentence.
This is the same Salviani work, Variarum lectionum de re medica, book 2, chapter 1.
Johann Lange's Epistolae medicinales includes the story of Menecrates styling himself Jupiter.
Albert Krantz's history of Denmark (Dania, part of his Chronica regnorum aquilonarium) fits the reference, and Krantz is cited alongside Surius on Hecla.
Jacob Coler wrote a treatise on the immortality of the soul. Labelled probable, which is a fair hedge.
Acosta's Historia natural y moral, book 3, chapter 9 describes the sickness that strikes travellers crossing Pariacaca.
Nicholas Hill's Philosophia Epicurea, Democritiana, Theophrastica (1601) is the work meant.
Plato discusses and divides hunting at the end of Laws book 7.
Jan Dubravius (Dubravius the Moravian), De piscinis (on fishponds).
'Of Wisdom' points to Pontano's De prudentia, and book 4 is plausible. Labelled probable.

Among Chrysostom's genuine Homilies on Matthew, homily 2 is on Matthew 1, not Matthew 3 (Matthew 3 comes in homilies 10–12). Burton's 'hom. 2 in 3 Mat.' may mean another homily or the Opus imperfectum, so this identification is uncertain.
'Like sheep they lie in the grave' is Psalm 49:14.
Ambrose's De Cain et Abel has only two books, so 'book 3' cannot be right as it stands. Also, the marked span includes 'Cain,', which belongs to Burton's sentence, not the reference.
Brasavola, Examen omnium simplicium medicamentorum.
Oswald Croll, Basilica chymica (1609).
Jean de Renou's Dispensatorium includes three books De materia medica, and book 3 covers animal remedies such as bezoar.
The French physician who wrote against antimony is Jacques Grévin: De venenis libri duo, with an attack on antimony.
Montalto's Archipathologia, on melancholy, is plausible for 'cap. 30'. Labelled probable.
No author is named at this point, so Crato is a guess. Consilium numbers as high as 285–286 fit Montanus's long numbered series of Consilia better than Crato's, which Burton usually cites by book.
Giulio Cesare Claudini's Responsionum et consultationum medicinalium liber, response 33, is correct.
Du Laurens does deal with love-melancholy in his Discourse, but in chapter 10, not chapter 5. The work or the Laurentius meant may be different, so the identification is uncertain.
Scaliger's Exotericae exercitationes, exercise 301 (on love), fits Burton's discussion of definitions of love.
Busbecq's Legationis Turcicae epistolae, letter 3, is correct for a report about the Grand Signior.
Francesco Barbaro's De re uxoria, book 1, chapter 5, is consistent with Burton's text.
Sirach 9:4 reads 'Use not much the company of a woman that is a singer', which matches the text.
Scherertz's Libellus consolatorius de spectris (1621) is a plausible work for a chapter on the night-goat (incubus), but I can't confirm the chapter number and the identification is unchecked.

Avicenna's chapter on love-melancholy (ilisci) is in the Canon, book 3, fen 1, tractate 4, and the write-out leaves that location out. Burton elsewhere gives the chapter as 23, so chapter 24 is uncertain.
The author is right, but the write-out names no work. Lemnius wrote several books, so 'book 1, chapter 6' is incomplete as a reference.
Bellarmine's De monachis (in the Controversiae), chapter 38, is correct for his discussion of broken vows of chastity.
The marked reference wrongly includes Burton's own words 'by which a man is inclined…'. Also, charity is treated in II-II, question 23, of the Summa, not I-II as the write-out gives it.
Acosta's Historia natural y moral de las Indias, book 5, chapters 1–4, on idolatry and the Devil's imitation of worship, is correct.
Acosta, book 5, chapter 20, on Mexican human sacrifice, is correct.
Girolamo Dandini's commentary on Aristotle's De anima, book 3, is correct, and it is properly marked probable.

Burton's '2. 2ae' is a slip. II–II q. 40 is on war (a. 4: whether it is lawful to fight on holy days). 'Recessus a re desiderata' comes from I–II q. 40 a. 4, which asks whether despair is contrary to hope. The written-out form should give I–II as the place, not as a hedged alternative under 'sure'.
Caelius Secundus Curio, De amplitudine beati regni Dei (1554), which Burton cites for the larger number of the saved.
1 Peter 1:6: 'Wherein ye greatly rejoice, though now for a season… ye are in heaviness.'
Proverbs 26:12: 'Seest thou a man wise in his own conceit?' This follows Proverbs 3:7, 'Be not wise in thine own eyes.'
The written-out form matches Burton's reference, 'lib. 2'. I can't confirm from memory that this plague is told in Book 2 of the Historia nova; it may be Book 1.
Pausanias, Book 7 (Achaica), tells of the river Selemnus that cures lovers (7.23).
The note points to Seneca's Consolatio ad Marciam, written to Marcia on her son Metilius' death. 'Cujusque ferae pabulum' comes from it.
Abu Ma'shar (787–886), the Persian astrologer who worked at Baghdad, is known for his theory of great conjunctions.
Alessandro Massaria of Vicenza (1510–1598) was professor of medicine at Padua and wrote Practica medica.
Al-Kindi (c. 801–c. 873) wrote on the degrees and doses of compound medicines, which fits 'Opusc. de Dos.'
Anteros is the god of returned love, son of Aphrodite and brother of Eros.
Anytus was Socrates' accuser. Plutarch's Life of Alcibiades makes him Alcibiades' lover and tells the story of the plate.
The quotation 'virgo formosa, etsi oppido pauper…' comes from Apuleius' Apologia (ch. 92).
Araspas is the Mede in the Cyropaedia who guarded Panthea and fell in love with her.
Ardres in Pas-de-Calais is right; the 1520 Field of the Cloth of Gold met between Guînes and Ardres. Burton's own note gives 1519.
Aristarchus of Samos (c. 310–c. 230 BC) proposed that the earth moves round the sun.
Barry Island lies off Glamorgan. Giraldus tells of the smith's-forge sounds heard from a cleft in its cliff.
William the Conqueror founded Battle Abbey on the site of the Battle of Hastings. The '1347' note belongs to the Calais story that follows.
Jean-Baptiste Besard of Besançon, lutenist and physician, wrote Antrum philosophicum (1617).
Q. Fulvius Flaccus, censor in 174–173 BC, took the marble tiles of Juno Lacinia's temple for Fortuna Equestris and later went mad (Livy 42.3, 42.28).
Correct identification and dates; Burton cites De occulta philosophia lib. 1.
Leonhard Culmann (c.1498–1562), Nuremberg Lutheran pastor and writer of devotional and school works; 'probable' is a fair hedge.
Divus Hadrianus, the deified emperor Hadrian; the reign dates are right.
Andreas Dudith (1533–1589), a bishop who left the Church and later lived among Protestants; Monau wrote letters to him.
Gunter (1581–1626), Christ Church man and Gresham professor of astronomy; his Canon triangulorum (logarithmic sines and tangents) came out in 1620.
Emilia Pia (d. 1528), who speaks in Castiglione's Courtier.
Ionian city opposite Chios, home of the Erythraean Sibyl; it fits Burton's list of Apollo's oracle sites.
The son of Oedipus who killed Polynices and was killed by him in single combat.
A fictional letter-writer in Aristaenetus, as Burton's 'Euhemerus in Aristaenetus… Epist. 12' indicates. It is hedged as 'probable', which suits the evidence.
The gens Fabia; traditionally 306 men fell at the Cremera in 477 BC (Ovid, Fasti 2).
Johannes Garcaeus the younger (1530–1574), Lutheran theologian and astrologer; Astrologiae methodus (1576).
Ghismonda, daughter of Tancredi of Salerno, in Decameron IV.1; her lover Guiscardo is killed by her father.
Gualtherus Bruele, Flemish physician, author of Praxis medicinae theorica et empirica.
The supposed Arab author of the purgative confectio Hamech; suitably hedged as 'probable'.
Girolamo Menghi (1529–1609), Franciscan exorcist, author of Flagellum daemonum.
Hippolyt von Colli (1561–1612), Zurich-born jurist and Palatine counsellor, wrote Incrementa urbium (1600), which matches Burton's 'de increm. urb.'
Lucian's Gallus, where the cock says it was once Pythagoras and before that Euphorbus. This fits the passage.
Euripides' Phoenissae. Polynices' exchange with Jocasta about exile, and his saying that one must play the fool with fools, are both in it.
Johannes Voschius wrote a De peste (late 16th century). The Low Countries origin is less certain, but the claim is properly marked probable.
Lelio dalla Fonte of Gubbio, physician. His Consultationes medicae were published in 1608. Correct.
John Leech (Leochaeus), Scottish Neo-Latin poet, whose love poems are addressed to Panthea. The probable hedge is fitting.
The youth of Plato's Lysis, named here alongside Phaedrus, Agathon and Charmides. Correct.
Johann Friedrich Matenesius of Cologne wrote De luxu et abusu vestium nostri temporis (1612). This matches the sidenote.
Mainz. Boniface was its archbishop and he challenged Virgil of Salzburg over the Antipodes.
Musonius Rufus, Stoic philosopher. His discourses on marriage are preserved in Stobaeus. Correct.

Athenian general who died in 413 BC; his superstitious delay after the eclipse ruined the Sicilian expedition. Burton is wrong that he was ostracised (that was Hyperbolus), but the person is correctly identified.
Drake's name (1579) for the California coast. Burton's sidenote cites Drake's voyage and the cold weather there.
Parthenis is a lovesick letter-writer in Aristaenetus' Love Letters, which is the work Burton cites.
Persinna, queen of Ethiopia in Heliodorus' Aethiopica, gave birth to the white Charicleia after looking at a picture of Andromeda.
Piotr Włostowic (Dunin), Silesian magnate who died in 1153, was blinded by Władysław II after a quarrel that began with a jest about their wives. Cromer tells the story.
The sidenote 'Pharmacop.' plus 'Quercetan' points to Du Chesne's Pharmacopoea dogmaticorum restituta (Paris, 1607), which praises vinum helleboratum and scilliticum.
Polynices is the son of Oedipus and Jocasta. In Euripides' Phoenissae he talks with Jocasta about the miseries of exile, and he and Eteocles kill each other.
Protervia (wantonness) is one of the minor Roman deities and personified qualities in Burton's list, which comes from Augustine and Giraldi.
Nicolaus Reimers (Raimarus) Ursus (1551–1600) had a geo-heliocentric system and a priority dispute with Tycho Brahe.
Roger, Bishop of Salisbury (d. 1139), was justiciar to Henry I and built Sherborne and Devizes. Stephen arrested him and seized his goods and castles; Newburgh and Camden tell the story.
This is the Regimen sanitatis Salernitanum. Johannes Curio's commentary on it is the one Burton cites.
Sesostris is the legendary Egyptian conqueror in Herodotus and Diodorus. The figure is linked to the Senusret pharaohs.

These are Acosta's Peruvian sierras (mountain zone), and the claim is hedged as probable. One flaw in the wording: Acosta's llanos are the coastal plains themselves, not a separate zone, and the Andes are a distinct range.
This is a Du Chesne (Quercetanus) spagyric pharmacopoeia, which goes with his 'responsio ad Aubertum'. The exact work is uncertain, and the claim is suitably hedged as probable.
In Book 2 of Heliodorus's Aethiopica, Calasiris tells how the Thracian courtesan Rhodopis tempted him at Memphis.
Petrus Thyraeus SJ (1546–1601) wrote De locis infestis (1598).
In Book 3 of the Cyropaedia, Tigranes, son of the Armenian king, asks his wife what she thought of Cyrus. She says she looked only at her husband.
Timothy Bright (c. 1551–1615) wrote A Treatise of Melancholie (1586).
Plutarch's Life of Alcibiades says Alcibiades seduced Timaea, wife of Agis II, and fathered Leotychides.
In the elder Seneca's Controversiae 6.8, a Vestal is accused of writing the line 'Felices nuptae! moriar nisi nubere dulce est'.
Aelian, Varia historia 9.7 (Xanthippe on Socrates' unchanging face). Burton's English renders the whole note.
Burton's English renders 'necessarium accidens decrepitis, et inseparabile' in full.
Burton's English renders the note, with his usual freedom ('nollet uti Venere' becomes 'would neither marry nor use the stews'). Nothing is left untranslated.
Burton's English renders the whole note, clause by clause.
'Terror in sapiente esse non debet' is rendered by 'will exclude fear from a wise man'.

Burton's English renders the note: 'bonae' is 'both good' just before the marker, 'si rectam rationem sequuntur' is 'if they be moderate', and 'malae si exorbitant' is 'pernicious if they be exorbitant'.
Burton's English covers 'nullo temporis momento quiesco…desidero'. The translation of the remaining 'per diversa loca vagor' is accurate.
Burton's English renders 'hac correpti non cogitant de medela' ('those seized by it do not think of a cure').
Burton's English renders 'jure privilegiandi, qui ob commune bonum abbreviant sibi vitam'.

Burton's English renders 'exiliit de lecto' and 'furentem non capiebat aula'. 'Indignatione nimia furens, animique impotens' is rendered by 'out of an angry fit, became mad' just before the marker. Nothing is left untranslated.
Note: 'so that voices striking bare walls might rebound sweeter and sharper' — Burton's 'clearer, by reason of the reverberation of the wall' renders it.
Burton's sentence renders the note fully: common disease, useful to consider its accidents, danger to the ignorant.
Exact rendering.

The note's sense (bad angels once named Jupiter etc., now St Sebastian, Barbara) is rendered by this sentence together with the preceding 'called heretofore Apollo…'; nothing substantive is left over.
'diversity of meats … prolong their meals' renders 'diversa nutrientia simul adjungere, et comedendi tempus prorogare'.
Aquae Porrectanae = Porrectan baths.
Exact rendering of the note.
'Circa hortos Epicuri frequenter' rendered by 'frequently seen in Epicurus' garden'.
Burton's sentence translates the whole note.
First sentence rendered by Burton; the verse 'Ingenio pollet cui vim natura negavit' is correctly translated.
'ob periculum suffocationis' rendered; 'Ab arte ideo rejiciendum' correctly translated as the remainder.
Exact rendering.
Burton's recipe renders the note clause by clause.
Flowers listed match (alibeae/althaea = mallows, capitis vervecum = wether's head); 'decocto' is implied by 'irrigations'.
Burton renders most items; the omitted 'viribus retinendis' and 'calorem innatum fovet' are correctly translated in the rest.

Burton's 'refrigerate the face' renders 'faciei prospiciendum ut ipsa refrigeretur'. He turns drinking into washing, and the translation correctly gives the rest: both ends served by often drinking the waters.
'All their study… fat, and then the cure is ended' renders both clauses: 'studium sit omne ut… impinguetur' and 'pingues… illico sani sunt'.
The English renders the dropax of pitch and oil of rue applied to the stomach and metaphrenum. Leaving out 'navali' (ship's pitch) and 'toti' is a minor looseness.
'Blame… rashness… love's enticements' renders 'ne quis temere… de amorum lenociniis'. The translation of the rest, 'of its practice, of fornications, adulteries, etc.', is accurate.
A faithful, slightly expanded rendering of 'terram non vis malam, malam segetem, sed bonam arborem, equum bonum'.

The note's 'nihil forma divinius, augustius, pretiosius… cujus vires hinc facile intelliguntur' is rendered within the span. The span runs across Burton's own Latin addition, but it has to, because the span is continuous.
'Saw in his scarfs… robes and coronet, quite mad' renders 'amictum chlamyde et coronis… ex potestate mentis excidit'.
A close rendering of Jerome on Blaesilla. 'By her temperance' freely renders 'se vincendo in hac parte'.
'Companion of all filthy delights… not easily told what inconveniences… talk… monstrous gestures' renders the whole note.
'Innocently to accuse the best… thing that belongs to mortal men' renders the note exactly.
'A King's Palace was not so diligently attended… as my house' renders 'regum palatium non tam diligenti custodia… ac aedes meas stipabant'.
The physicians' advice to marry or use coition, or else die, and his fearless choice of death, are fully rendered.
'Have no commerce' renders 'noli societatem habere'. 'With a single man' fills out the '&c.'
'Lest she be reputed… malapert and wanton, if she… make her own choice' renders 'ne appetentiae procacioris reputetur auctor'.
'Thou rangest like a Town Bull' renders 'vaga libidine… rapiaris', and 'why art thou so incensed if she tread awry' renders 'cur si… aberret… insanias'.
Burton's sentence fully renders the note: she revealed the trick, and it was silence, not the water, that calmed his anger.
Burton gives a faithful English version of Ambrose's sentence, so nothing is left over.
The note (Sibyls, Pythians and prophets who divine are all melancholy fanatics) is rendered by the Fracastorius clause.
The English covers the animals, fishes, birds and wine; 'mactabuntur' (slaughtered) is implied by 'banquet'. Close enough.

The translation is accurate, but the note only says 'In 17. Johannis' and does not name Luther. Its marker is at the Jerome quotation, which it does not match, so the note may be misplaced. Naming Luther with full certainty is not supported.

The quoted English leaves out 'tu tantum doceri te sine, manum ejus ne repelle' (only let yourself be taught; do not push his hand away). Burton renders it loosely as 'Submit thyself unto him', but that comes before the marker, and the translation of the rest is null.
Burton's words render the note: the ancients set this herb in churchyards because...
Isaiah 50:4 ('the tongue of the learned... a word... to him that is weary') is the verse Burton quotes.
Burton's English renders the Philo note adequately.
'Lupum auribus tenent' means 'they hold a wolf by the ears', which Burton renders exactly.
